a: ten weeks of years
t: Seventy years in Egypt with Joseph
p: A week of years is seven years, so ten of them are seventy: the years Joseph lived after Jacob came to Egypt.
b: A "week of years" is seven years, and the book counts all history in them and in jubilees of forty-nine years. Ten weeks are seventy years. Charles 1902 reckons by the book's own dates that Joseph died seventy years after Jacob arrived in Egypt, and that Joseph had already ruled ten years when his father came. So "all the days of Joseph's life" here means the rest of his life in Egypt with his family. Genesis gives no such number: it says only that the Israelites "were fruitful and swarmed" (Exodus 1:7).
orig: ወዐሠርተ ፡ ሱባዔ ፡ ዓመታት (wäʿäśärtä subaʿe ʿamätat), "and ten weeks of years"

a: All of them were of one heart
t: Compared with the Bible: a family at peace
p: Exodus says Israel grew. Jubilees adds that the brothers loved and helped one another.
b: Exodus 1:7 tells only of growth. Jubilees adds a picture of a united family: brother loves brother and each helps the other. After the long story of the brothers' hatred and Joseph's sale (Genesis 37), which this book also tells at 34:10-19, this goes beyond the Bible and gives a moral: while Israel holds together and Joseph lives, no harm comes (46:2). Compare Psalm 133:1. The Ge'ez ʿəruyanä bälbomu is "equal (or of one mind) in their heart."

a: There was no satan
t: "No satan": a word, not yet a name
p: Ge'ez säyṭan, from Hebrew satan "adversary." Here it means any accuser or harmful spirit, so it is lowercase.
b: The Ge'ez säyṭan comes from the Hebrew satan, "adversary" or "accuser." In Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3 the Hebrew has the article, "the Accuser," a title; in 1 Chronicles 21:1 it stands alone as a name. In Jubilees the word marks a state of the world: "no satan and nothing evil." The book uses the same pair for the days of blessing in 23:29, and again for Israel's future in 50:5. The Plain English Translation keeps it lowercase, since it is not the name of the book's chief evil spirit. That spirit is Mastema (48:2; 10:8), called Satan only once, at 10:11.

a: Joseph died at one hundred and ten years old
p: The age matches Genesis 50:26, and 17 + 10 + 3 + 80 adds up to 110.
b: Genesis 50:26 says, "Joseph died, one hundred and ten years old." Jubilees splits the years: seventeen in Canaan (Genesis 37:2, "When Joseph was seventeen years old"), ten as a slave and three in prison, which makes thirteen years before he "was thirty when he stood before Pharaoh" (Genesis 41:46), and eighty years ruling. The sum, 17 + 10 + 3 + 80, is exactly 110. The book often fills in such arithmetic the Bible leaves implied. The slave-and-prison split comes from Jubilees itself (39:5-14 tells it).

a: carry his bones with them
p: Genesis 50:25 has the oath, Exodus 13:19 keeps it, and Hebrews 11:22 calls it faith.
b: Joseph's last order is in Genesis 50:25: "carry my bones up from here." Moses kept it on the night of the Exodus: "Moses took Joseph's bones with him, because Joseph had made the sons of Israel swear an oath" (Exodus 13:19), and Joshua 24:32 tells of their burial at Shechem. The New Testament holds it up as faith: Joseph "gave instructions about his bones" (Hebrews 11:22). Jubilees adds the reason Joseph's body waited so long, a war that shut the road (46:6-9).

a: the Egyptians would not again bring him out
t: Compared with the Bible: why the bones waited
p: Egypt had escorted Jacob's body to Canaan (Genesis 50:7-13). Jubilees says it would not do so again for Joseph.
b: When Jacob died, Pharaoh's servants and "Chariots and horsemen" went up with Joseph to bury him in Canaan (Genesis 50:7-9). Genesis 50:26 says only that Joseph was laid in a coffin in Egypt. Jubilees explains the difference: Joseph knew that Egypt would not "again" carry a body out, because war had now closed the border. The explanation goes beyond the Bible but does not conflict with it, and it prepares for Exodus 13:19.

a: Makamaron, the king of Canaan
t: A war the Bible does not tell
p: No other source names Makamaron. Charles could not identify him; "Ermon" he took as Heroonpolis in the eastern Delta.
b: The Ge'ez name is Makamaron. Charles 1902 writes that he could not identify him, and that "Ermon" (Ge'ez ʾErmon) is Heroonpolis, a town near the desert on the eastern edge of the Nile Delta. He also notes that the Testaments of Simeon and of Benjamin mention a war between Egypt and Canaan at the time the patriarchs' bones were taken to Hebron, and that later Jewish retellings, beginning with Josephus, tell of other wars in Moses' youth; he judged Jubilees' war of Egypt and Canaan the oldest form. A king of Canaan "living in the land of Assyria" is strange, and no historical record matches the story.
r: Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs; Exodus 1:8-10

a: another, new king had become king of Egypt
p: Exodus 1:8 has a new king who did not know Joseph. In Jubilees the new king is a strong one who stops the invader.
b: Exodus 1:8 reads, "Then a new king came to the throne of Egypt, a king who did not know Joseph." Jubilees takes up "new king" but gives it a different setting: the new Pharaoh is strong enough to stop the Canaanite king at the border. In Jubilees the oppression grows out of war and fear of a fifth column (46:13), which Exodus 1:10 also mentions ("when a war comes, they will side with those who hate us").

a: in the forty-sixth jubilee, in the sixth week, in its second year
p: By the book's count this is year 2242 from creation.
b: Jubilees dates by jubilee, week and year. Forty-five full jubilees (45 x 49 = 2,205 years), five full weeks (35 years) and two years make the year 2242 from creation. Charles prints the same figure in his margin. The figure is the book's own arithmetic, not a date the Bible gives.

a: the bones of all of Jacob's sons except the bones of Joseph
p: Other Jewish writings tell the same story. Stephen says the fathers were laid at Shechem (Acts 7:16).
b: Genesis says nothing about where Joseph's brothers were buried. Charles 1902 points out that the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs say the brothers' bones were carried up to Hebron, secretly, during a war of Egypt and Canaan (Testament of Simeon 8; Testament of Benjamin 12), and that Josephus held that their descendants later buried them in Hebron. In Acts, Stephen says that "our ancestors" were "moved to Shechem and put in the tomb Abraham had paid silver for" (Acts 7:15-16). Charles thought Stephen depended on a tradition like this one, though the place differs: Jubilees says the double cave near Hebron, Stephen says Shechem.
r: Acts 7:15-16; Joshua 24:32; Genesis 50:13; Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs

a: the double cave
p: Ge'ez "the cave that is double" is the cave of Machpelah, where Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lay.
b: The Ge'ez says "the cave which is double." This is the cave of Machpelah near Hebron, which Abraham bought (Genesis 23:9) and where Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah and Jacob were buried (Genesis 49:29-32; Genesis 50:13). The Hebrew name Machpelah is close to a word for "double," and Jubilees uses that sense as its name for the cave.

a: Your father Amram
t: Amram, and the "you" of the book
p: The angel is talking to Moses. Amram is his father (Exodus 6:20); the Ge'ez spells him Abram here.
b: "Your father" reminds the reader that the whole book is the angel of the presence speaking to Moses on Sinai (1:27-2:1). From here to the end, the "you" is Moses. His father Amram is named in Exodus 6:20: "Amram took Jochebed, his father's sister, as his wife, and she bore him Aaron and Moses." The Ge'ez spells the name ʾÄbram here and ʿƎbran in 47:9. Charles 1902 notes the form Abram also in Philo and in one manuscript of the Greek Numbers 26:59, and (citing Beer) that no other source tells of Amram staying behind in Hebron.

a: He made an evil plan
p: The Ge'ez says only "he." The king of Canaan was just named, but the plotter must be Egypt's king, as in Exodus 1.
b: The verse begins with "he," and the last king named is the king of Canaan; who "shut the gates of Egypt" in 46:11 is just as unclear. The plotter is best taken as the king of Egypt: he speaks to "the people of Egypt" and builds cities "for Pharaoh" (46:14), as in Exodus 1:9-11. The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez "he" rather than guessing.

a: Come, let us outsmart them
p: Close to Exodus 1:9-10, with one change: Israel's hearts are turned toward Canaan.
b: Pharaoh's words follow Exodus 1:9-10: "Look, the Israelite people have grown bigger and stronger than we are. Come on, let us outsmart them" (Exodus 1:9-10). Jubilees adds the reason for his fear: the Israelites' "hearts and their faces are turned toward the land of Canaan," where some of them now live (46:10). In the book's story, Israel's longing for the land of promise is what makes Egypt afraid.

a: strong cities
t: "Strong cities," as the Greek has it
p: The Hebrew of Exodus 1:11 says "supply cities"; the Greek Bible says "strong cities," and so does Jubilees.
b: In Exodus 1:11 the Hebrew calls Pithom and Rameses "supply cities" (miskenot, "store cities"). Charles 1902 notes that the Greek translation renders the word "strong cities" (πόλεις ὀχυραί) there and in 2 Chronicles 8:4, and the Ge'ez of Jubilees has the same sense, ʾähgurä ṣənuʿatä. The rebuilding of "every wall and every rampart that had fallen down" is Jubilees' own addition: Egypt fortifies itself after its defeat (46:11).

a: however much they mistreated them, that much more they multiplied
p: The same turn as Exodus 1:12.
b: Exodus 1:12: "Yet however hard they pressed them down, that much more they multiplied, and that much more they burst out." Jubilees keeps the pattern: the harder Egypt pushes, the more Israel grows, a sign that God's promise to Abraham (Genesis 15:5; Genesis 22:17) is working.

a: came to loathe
p: The Ge'ez verb comes from a root meaning "unclean": Egypt treated Israel as something filthy.
b: The Ge'ez yastärakʷsəwomu comes from the root of rəkʷs, "uncleanness" (the word in 50:5), and means to regard something as filthy or loathsome. The Hebrew of Exodus 1:12 uses a different word, which the site's Exodus renders "grew sick with fear." Jubilees leans toward disgust rather than dread.

a: your father came from the land of Canaan
t: Amram's return and Moses' birth year
p: By the book's dates, Amram came back to Egypt in year 2303 and Moses was born in 2330.
b: By the book's formula, the seventh year of the seventh week of the forty-seventh jubilee is year 2303 from creation (46 x 49 + 6 x 7 + 7), forty years after the war of 46:9. Moses is born in the sixth year of the fourth week of the forty-eighth jubilee, year 2330. Charles prints the same figures. Jubilees thus makes Amram one of the few who stayed in Canaan (46:10) and came back. Exodus 2:1 says only, "A man from Levi's family went and took a daughter of Levi as his wife."

a: into the river
p: Exodus 1:22 sends every son into the Nile. Jubilees, like Exodus 1:22, aims at the boys.
b: Exodus 1:22: "Every son who is born, you must throw into the Nile." The Ge'ez says "the river," the usual word for the Nile, and "every male." Jubilees skips the midwives of Exodus 1:15-21 altogether and moves straight from forced labor to the drowning of the boys.

a: for seven months
t: Seven months, ten months, ten plagues
p: A Byzantine chronicler, quoting "the Little Genesis," says the babies were thrown in for ten months.
b: The Greek chronicler George Cedrenus, quoting "the Little Genesis" (an old name for Jubilees), says the Hebrew babies were thrown into the river for only ten months, until Moses was taken up by the queen, and that for this reason ten plagues came on Egypt in ten months (Charles 1902 prints the Greek, "μόνους δέκα μῆνας," "only ten months"). The two counts fit: seven months until Moses' birth, then three months of hiding (47:3), make ten. Cedrenus also has the thousand drowned Egyptians for each baby (48:14).

a: people reported her
t: Compared with the Bible: why the hiding failed
p: Exodus says she "could not hide him any longer." Jubilees says someone informed on her.
b: Exodus 2:3 says only, "But she could not hide him any longer." Jubilees gives a reason: wänägäru bäʾnətiha, "they told about her," that is, someone reported her. This goes beyond the Bible. The Hebrews' danger came not only from Pharaoh but from neighbors who talked.

a: pitch and asphalt
t: Two Greek words in the Ge'ez
p: Ge'ez pisa and ʾasfaliṭo are the Greek words for pitch and asphalt: a trace of the Greek copy behind the Ge'ez.
b: The two coatings, pisa and ʾasfaliṭo, are Greek words (pissa, "pitch," and asphaltos, "asphalt") taken over into Ge'ez. They are one of many small signs that the Ge'ez Jubilees was translated from a Greek copy, which was itself made from the Hebrew. Exodus 2:3 has "smeared it with tar and pitch."

a: She put you in it for seven days
t: Compared with the Bible: a week by the river
p: The week in the reeds, the night feedings and Miriam scaring off birds are all added to Exodus 2.
b: In Exodus 2:3-5 the basket is set in the reeds and Pharaoh's daughter finds it, with no time given. Jubilees adds a week: the mother comes by night to nurse the baby, and his sister guards him by day "from the birds." Exodus 2:4 says only, "His sister took her place far off, to learn what would be done to him." The additions go beyond the Bible without conflicting with it. Seven days is a favorite span in the book.

a: your sister Miriam
p: Exodus 2 does not name the sister. Jubilees does, as Numbers 26:59 does elsewhere.
b: Exodus 2:4-8 never names Moses' sister. Jubilees names her (Ge'ez Marya), as the Bible does later: "Miriam the prophet, Aaron's sister" in Exodus 15:20, and "their sister Miriam" in Numbers 26:59. Most Jewish and Christian readers have made the same identification.

a: Tarmut, Pharaoh's daughter
t: Tarmut, the princess with a name
p: Exodus does not name her. Jubilees calls her Tarmut; Josephus calls her Thermouthis.
b: The Bible never names Pharaoh's daughter. Jubilees calls her Tärmut. Charles 1902 notes the same name in the Syriac fragment of Jubilees and "Thermouthis" in Josephus (Antiquities 2.9) and in Syncellus.

a: her Hebrew women
p: Charles, following Dillmann, thinks a Greek word for "maids" was misread as "Hebrew women." The Latin has "maid."
b: The Ge'ez says ʿəbrawiyatiha, "her Hebrew women," and has them fetch the baby. In Exodus 2:5 she "sent her slave woman." Charles 1902 notes that the Latin of Jubilees has the singular "maid" (Greek ἄβρα), as do the Hebrew, Samaritan, Greek and Latin texts of Exodus, and writes, as Dillmann saw, that the Ge'ez is a mistranslation of the Greek ἄβραις, "maids," which a translator read as "Hebrew women"; the plural is also found in the Syriac of Exodus 2:5. If so, the error came in when the Greek was turned into Ge'ez. The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez as it stands.

a: one of the Hebrew women
p: Almost word for word Exodus 2:7.
b: Exodus 2:7 reads, "Should I go and find a nursing mother from the Hebrew women for you, so she can nurse the child for you?" Jubilees follows the Bible closely here, as it does in most of Moses' early story, adding only the names (Tarmut, Miriam, Jochebed) and the dates.

a: your mother, Jochebed
p: Exodus 2 leaves her unnamed; Exodus 6:20 and Numbers 26:59 name her.
b: In Exodus 2 Moses' mother has no name. Jubilees uses the name given later: "The name of Amram's wife was Jochebed, daughter of Levi" (Numbers 26:59; compare Exodus 6:20). The Ge'ez is ʾIyokbet.

a: Your father Amram taught you writing
t: Compared with the Bible: who taught Moses?
p: Acts says Moses learned Egypt's wisdom. Jubilees says his Hebrew father taught him to write.
b: Stephen says, "Moses was schooled in all the wisdom of the Egyptians" (Acts 7:22), and Philo and Clement of Alexandria describe his Egyptian teachers. Charles 1902 notes that Jubilees takes another view: Moses' own father taught him writing. This fits the book's chain of sacred books, passed from Enoch through Noah, Abraham and Jacob to Levi and his sons (45:16), and Amram was of Levi's line. Exodus says nothing about Moses' schooling, so neither view conflicts with Exodus, but they point in different directions: one stresses Egyptian learning, the other an unbroken Hebrew tradition.

a: three weeks of years
t: Moses' age in weeks of years
p: Three weeks of years is twenty-one: Moses enters the court at 21 and leaves it at 42.
b: Three weeks of years are twenty-one years, so Moses comes to court at about 21, stays three more weeks (47:10), and leaves at 42. That agrees with the book's dates: born 2330 (47:1), fled 2372 (48:1). Stephen gives a different round number: "As he was turning forty, he made up his mind to go and see how his brothers, the Israelites, were doing" (Acts 7:23). Exodus 2:11 says only that Moses "had grown up."

a: You killed him and hid him in the sand
t: Compared with the Bible: no glance around
p: Jubilees tells Exodus 2:11-12 but leaves out Moses looking this way and that.
b: Exodus 2:12 says Moses "turned this way and that and saw no one there" before he struck. Jubilees leaves out the glance, which readers have long taken to show that Moses knew he was doing something hidden. It also calls the beaten man "your companion." The killing is told without blame, as it is in Acts 7:24, which says he "paid back the wrong done to the beaten-down man."

a: Who put you as a chief and a judge over us?
p: Exodus 2:14 and Acts 7:27 give the same question. Jubilees leaves out Pharaoh's search for Moses.
b: The question is that of Exodus 2:14, "Who put you as a chief and a judge over us? Are you saying you will kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?" and Acts 7:27. Exodus then says Pharaoh "looked for a way to kill Moses" (Exodus 2:15). Jubilees skips that: Moses runs "because of what he said," and the threat that matters in the next chapter is not Pharaoh's but Mastema's.

a: five weeks of years and one year
p: The dates in this verse imply 38 years in Midian. Charles thinks "one year" was miscopied from "three years."
b: Moses leaves in year 2372 (the sixth year of the third week of the forty-ninth jubilee) and comes back in 2410 (the second year of the second week of the fiftieth). That is 38 years, but "five weeks of years and one year" is 36. Charles 1902 judged "one year" a copying error for "three years." With 38 years, Moses is 80 when he returns (2410 minus 2330), which matches Exodus 7:7: "Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three, when they spoke to Pharaoh."
orig: ኀምስተ ፡ ሱባዔ ፡ ወዓመተ ፡ አሐደ (ḫämsətä subaʿe wäʿamätä ʾäḥädä)

a: what was spoken to you on Mount Sinai
p: Exodus 3:1 calls the mountain Horeb. Jubilees calls it Sinai, as most readers take them to be one place.
b: This points to God's call at the burning bush (Exodus 3-4). Exodus 3:1 says Moses "came to God's mountain, toward Horeb." Jubilees calls it Mount Sinai, the place where the angel is now speaking (1:2-4). Many readers, Jewish and Christian, take Horeb and Sinai as two names for the same mountain; some scholars think they were two traditions.

a: Prince Mastema
p: Ge'ez mäkʷännä mästema. Mastema leads the evil spirits; Greek writers spell him Mastiphat or Mastipham, the Latin Mastima.
b: The Ge'ez mäkʷännä mästema is "Prince Mastema" (see 10:8, where the book first names him, and 11:5 and 17:16, where he is first called Prince). He is the chief of the evil spirits whom God allowed to stay on earth after the Flood. Charles 1902 notes that the Latin spells him Mastima, the Greek chroniclers Syncellus and Cedrenus Μαστιφάμ and Μαστιφάτ, and that a medieval Hebrew Book of Noah has sar ha-mastema, "prince of enmity." The Plain English Translation keeps the name Mastema; it writes "Satan" only at 10:11, where the Ge'ez itself has säyṭan. In 48:9, 12 and 15 Charles's manuscripts a and b have "the prince of the Mastema" (Charles 1902, note on 48:9).

a: what Prince Mastema wanted to do to you
t: Compared with the Bible: who attacked Moses at the inn?
p: Exodus 4:24 says the LORD sought to kill Moses. Jubilees gives the attack to Mastema, and the angel rescues Moses.
b: Exodus 4:24 is one of the strangest verses in the Bible: on the way back to Egypt, "the LORD met him and sought to kill him," until Zipporah circumcised their son. Jubilees changes the actor. It is Prince Mastema who wants to kill Moses, to protect the Egyptians, and the angel of the presence who rescues him (48:4). Zipporah and the circumcision vanish. Charles 1902 compares 1 Chronicles 21:1, where "Satan stood up against Israel" in place of 2 Samuel 24:1's "He stirred David up," and Jubilees' own retelling of Genesis 22:1 (17:16). He judged that Jubilees here "explains away" the meaning of Exodus, which other Jewish retellings, such as Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, keep. The book does the same in 48:17 and 49:2. This is a real conflict with the wording of Exodus, though not with its claim that God rules over both.

a: But I rescued you from his hand
p: The angel speaking to Moses says he himself saved Moses from Mastema.
b: The narrator is the angel of the presence (1:27; 2:1), who sometimes says "I" and sometimes "we" (48:10-11, 48:16). In Exodus 4:26 the attacker simply "let go of him." In Jubilees a good angel stands between Moses and the evil one, as the same angel does at the sea (48:13) and at the binding of Isaac (18:9). Compare "the angel of God" in Exodus 14:19.

a: He struck them and killed them with blood and frogs
t: The ten judgments in one breath
p: Jubilees lists all ten plagues of Exodus 7-12, with the death of the animals and the sores in a different order.
b: The list follows Exodus 7-12: blood (Exodus 7:14-25), frogs (Exodus 8:1-15), lice or gnats (Exodus 8:16-19), dog-flies, Exodus's swarm (Exodus 8:20-32), the sores (Exodus 9:8-12), the death of the animals (Exodus 9:1-7), hail (Exodus 9:13-35), locusts (Exodus 10:1-20), darkness (Exodus 10:21-29) and the firstborn (Exodus 11:1-12:30). Only the sores and the animals' death trade places. Charles 1902 notes that both the Ge'ez and the Latin lack a word before "their firstborn" (he supplied "the death of"), a sign of a gap in the Greek copy. Exodus 9:10 has the same picture of "sores bursting into blisters."

a: dog-flies
p: The Hebrew of Exodus 8:21 says only "the swarm." The Ge'ez says "dog-flies," a biting fly.
b: The Ge'ez ṣənṣənya kälb is "fly of the dog," a biting fly that plagues animals. The Hebrew of Exodus 8:21 has ʿarov, "the swarm," without saying what insects. Jubilees reads the swarm as dog-flies, the kind of guess every ancient translation had to make.

a: burned them with fire
t: Compared with the Bible: Egypt's gods burned
p: Exodus 12:12 promises judgment on Egypt's gods. Jubilees says God burned them.
b: Exodus 12:12: "And on all the gods of Egypt I will carry out judgments. I am the LORD." Numbers 33:4 repeats the promise. Jubilees makes the judgment concrete: the Lord "burned them with fire," as idols are burned in Deuteronomy 7:5 and Deuteronomy 7:25. The Bible never says how the judgment on Egypt's gods was carried out, so this goes beyond it.

a: which he made in a covenant with Abraham
p: God had promised Abraham that he would judge the nation that enslaved his offspring.
b: This points back to the covenant between the pieces: "But I will judge the nation they serve, and afterward they will come out with great wealth" (Genesis 15:14). Jubilees retells that covenant in chapter 14. The plagues are not random disasters but a promise kept, and the plunder of Egypt (48:18) fulfills the "great wealth." Jubilees calls the promise God's śərʿat, "ordinance," which he täkayädä with Abraham, a verb Leslau's dictionary gives as "make a covenant, make a pact." Charles 1902 renders "according to His covenant, which He had ordained with Abraham."
orig: ሥርዐቱ ፡ ዘተካየደ ፡ ምስለ ፡ አብርሃም (śərʿätu zätäkayädä məslä ʾäbrəham)

a: He helped the sorcerers of Egypt
p: Exodus 7-8 has Pharaoh's magicians copy the signs; 2 Timothy 3:8 names two of them. Jubilees puts Mastema behind them.
b: In Exodus the magicians "did the same with their spells" (Exodus 7:11; Exodus 7:22; Exodus 8:7), until the gnats defeated them (Exodus 8:18-19). Jubilees explains their power: Mastema helped them. Later Jewish tradition named two magicians, and Paul knows the names: "Jannes and Jambres stood against Moses" (2 Timothy 3:8). Jubilees uses the same word, "stood against" (yətqawämu), but gives no names.

a: We let them do the evil things
p: The angels allowed the magicians to cause plagues but never to cure them.
b: In Exodus the magicians can turn water to blood and bring up frogs (Exodus 7:22; Exodus 8:7), but they never remove a plague: Pharaoh has to ask Moses to pray (Exodus 8:8). Jubilees turns that observation into a rule. Evil can harm only as far as God's angels allow ("we let them"), and it has no power to heal. The same idea stands behind 10:10-13, where the angels teach Noah remedies against the spirits.

a: they could not stand their ground
p: Exodus 9:11: the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the sores.
b: Exodus 9:11: "The magicians were unable to stand before Moses because of the sores, since the sores had broken out on the magicians and on all Egypt." Jubilees adds why: "we made them lose the power to do even one sign." The angels, not the sores alone, end the magicians' contest. The verb ʾäḥgʷälnahomu is from ʾaḥgʷala, which Leslau's dictionary gives as "destroy, lose, make lose"; Charles 1902 renders "we destroyed them so that they could not perform a single sign."

a: was not put to shame
p: The Ge'ez reads "was not ashamed until he grew strong." Charles found it hard and suggested "because."
b: The Ge'ez says ʾiḫäfärä ... ʾəskä sobä ḫäyälä, "was not ashamed, until when he grew strong." Charles 1902 found that "fails to give a good sense" and suggested that the Hebrew behind it read "because" (ʿal-asher, על־אשר) instead of "until" (ʿad-asher, עד־אשר): "was not put to shame, because he took courage." The Plain English Translation takes ʾəskä in its sense "so far as": Mastema was not shamed by his defeats, so much so that he grew bold again. Compare 18:12, where Mastema "was put to shame" when Isaac was spared.
orig: ኢኀፈረ ፡ መኰንነ ፡ መስቴማ ፡ እስከ ፡ ሶበ ፡ ኀየለ (ʾiḫäfärä mäkʷännä mästema ʾəskä sobä ḫäyälä)

a: through the middle of the sea as if through dry land
p: As in Exodus 14:22 and Hebrews 11:29.
b: Exodus 14:22: "The Israelites went into the middle of the sea on dry ground." Hebrews 11:29 says they went through "as if it were dry ground." Jubilees adds the angel standing between the camps (Exodus 14:19-20 has "the angel of God" and the pillar of cloud moving behind Israel) and calls the danger "his hand," Mastema's, as well as the Egyptians'.

a: Just as the people of Egypt had thrown their children into the river
p: Egypt drowned Israel's babies, so Egypt's army drowned in the sea.
b: The punishment fits the crime: those who threw babies into the river are thrown into the sea. Charles 1902 calls this the "law of retaliation" also stated in Wisdom of Solomon 11:16, "what a person sins with, he is punished with," and points to Wisdom of Solomon 18:5, where God "wiped them out together in the mighty water" for their plan "to kill the babies of your holy ones." Exodus does not draw the link in so many words, though Jethro comes close when he says of the LORD, "He proved it when they acted with such pride against this people" (Exodus 18:11). The thousand-for-one figure is Jubilees' own, and Cedrenus repeats it from the Little Genesis.
r: Exodus 1:22; Exodus 14:28; Exodus 18:11; Wisdom of Solomon 11:16; Wisdom of Solomon 18:5

a: a million
p: Ge'ez "a hundred ʾəlf." The word can mean a thousand or ten thousand; here it is ten thousand, so the sum is a million.
b: The Ge'ez is məʾtä ʾəlfä, "a hundred ʾəlf." Leslau's Comparative Dictionary of Ge'ez gives ʾəlf as "thousand, ten thousand, myriad." The same verse writes a thousand as ʿäśärtu məʾt, "ten hundred," so here ʾəlf is best taken as ten thousand, and a hundred of them make 1,000,000, the figure Charles 1902 prints. If ʾəlf meant a thousand, the sum would be 100,000. Either way the number stands for a whole army destroyed, not a count.

a: strong, bold men
t: A phrase no one is sure of
p: The Ge'ez adds words that are partly unclear, roughly "and those ... three ... are bold." Charles: "strong and energetic."
b: After "ten hundred strong men" the Ge'ez adds wäʾlähi śälästä yədalägu. The last word is from the verb dalaga, which Leslau's dictionary gives as "be bold, be energetic," with "be ardent for battle" among its senses; the Plain English Translation renders it "bold," and Charles has "strong and energetic men." The words before it, wäʾlähi śälästä, "and those ... three," give no clear sense and are left untranslated. The Greek of Cedrenus has just "a thousand strong Egyptian men" (Charles 1902). See the theory note on the same verse.

a: A thousand strong, bold men
p: The puzzling "three" may reflect the Hebrew shalish, the officer of a chariot crew.
b: This is Claude's own suggestion. Exodus 14:7, the verse about Pharaoh's chariots at the sea, has shalishim, "officers" (the site's "with officers over all of it"). The Hebrew word looks as if it is built on "three." If the Hebrew of Jubilees used that word here, a translator who took it as "three" could have left the odd śälästä, "three," in the Ge'ez. The idea rests only on the shape of the words; it would mean "a thousand strong men and the chariot officers perished." No edition read here proposes it.

a: Prince Mastema was bound and locked up
p: Mastema is bound for the days of the Exodus so he cannot accuse Israel. Revelation 20 binds the dragon for a thousand years.
b: In Jubilees the angels bind Mastema from the fourteenth to the eighteenth of the first month so that he "could not accuse" Israel, then loose him (48:16). The book's idea of an accuser is old: "the Accuser" stands before God in Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3:1. The binding of an evil leader for a set time comes back in the New Testament: an angel "seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years" (Revelation 20:2), and "After that he must be let loose for a short time" (Revelation 20:3). Revelation 12:10 calls him "the accuser of our brothers and sisters." Compare also the angels kept in chains in Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4, and 1 Enoch 10:4.
r: Job 1:6-12; Zechariah 3:1; Revelation 20:2-3; Revelation 12:10; Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4; 1 Enoch 10:4

a: On the fourteenth day, the fifteenth, the sixteenth, the seventeenth and the eighteenth
p: The Passover on the 14th, the march from the 15th to the 18th, the pursuit from the 19th.
b: Jubilees gives a day-by-day plan: Mastema is bound on the fourteenth, the day of the Passover and the plunder (48:18); Israel marches from the fifteenth to the eighteenth; on the nineteenth the evil powers are let loose and the Egyptians pursue. Charles 1902 notes that Josephus also has Israel leave on the fifteenth, and (citing Beer) that the rabbinic commentary Mekhilta has the Egyptians pursue from the nineteenth. Exodus gives no dates between the departure (Exodus 12:41; Numbers 33:3, "on the fifteenth day of the first month") and the sea.

a: made them bold
t: Compared with the Bible: who hardened Egypt?
p: In Exodus 14 the LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart. Here "he" seems to be Mastema, yet the strength comes "by the Lord."
b: Exodus 14:8: "The LORD made the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt stubborn, and he chased after the Israelites." In Jubilees the subject is "he," and the last one named is Mastema and his powers (48:16). Charles 1902 read it so: the book again "attributes to the immediate agency of Mastema" what Exodus gives to God (as in 48:2). Yet the next words say the Egyptians "were made bold by the Lord our God, so that he could strike" them. Jubilees keeps God in charge while moving the hardening one step away from him. On the Bible's own picture, see the topic on hardening of the heart.

a: strip the Egyptians
p: Exodus says Israel "stripped Egypt bare." Jubilees calls it payment for the years of slavery.
b: Exodus 3:22 and Exodus 12:35-36 tell how Israel asked for silver, gold and clothing: "So they stripped Egypt bare." Readers have long asked whether this was fair. Jubilees answers twice: it was "in return for the slavery they had forced on them," and Mastema was bound that day so that he "could not accuse" Israel for it. The Wisdom of Solomon gives the same answer: wisdom "paid the holy ones the wages of their labor" (Wisdom of Solomon 10:17). Genesis 15:14 had promised "great wealth." Jubilees adds bronze to the silver and gold.
r: Exodus 3:21-22; Exodus 11:2; Exodus 12:35-36; Genesis 15:14; Wisdom of Solomon 10:17

a: empty-handed
p: God's promise at the bush, Exodus 3:21.
b: "Then, when you go, you will not go empty-handed" (Exodus 3:21). The chapter ends where Moses' call began: what was "spoken to you on Mount Sinai" (48:2) has come true. The Ge'ez ʿəraqomu is literally "naked."

a: the Passover
p: Ge'ez fasika (here) and paska (49:2 on) both come from the Greek pascha, from Hebrew pesach.
b: The Ge'ez uses two spellings: fasika here and p̣aska or p̣äskä from 49:2 on. Both come from the Greek pascha, which renders the Hebrew pesach. Paul uses the Greek word of Christ: "For our Passover, Christ, has been slaughtered" (1 Corinthians 5:7).

a: on the evening of the fifteenth
p: The lamb is slaughtered on the 14th; the meal is eaten that night, which already counts as the 15th.
b: Jubilees, like the Bible, counts a day from sunset. The lamb is killed on the fourteenth "before evening comes," and eaten after sunset, which is already the fifteenth. Exodus 12:6-8 and Leviticus 23:5-6 say the same in other words: "In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, between the two evenings, is the LORD's Passover" (Leviticus 23:5), and "On the fifteenth day of this month is the LORD's Feast of Unleavened Bread" (Leviticus 23:6).

a: all the powers of Mastema
t: Compared with the Bible: who struck the firstborn?
p: Exodus says the LORD struck the firstborn and kept "the destroyer" out of Israel's houses. Jubilees sends Mastema's powers.
b: Exodus 12:29: "In the middle of the night the LORD struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt." Exodus 12:23 also speaks of "the destroyer": "He will not let the destroyer come into your houses to strike you." Jubilees gives the killing to "the powers of Mastema" (as Charles 1902 notes, in the manner of 48:2 and 48:17), yet they are "sent," and in 49:4 it is "the powers of the Lord" that pass over Israel. The evil powers act only on God's errand. The New Testament also speaks of "the one who destroyed the firstborn" (Hebrews 11:28) and "the Destroyer" (1 Corinthians 10:10).

a: the firstborn of the captive slave woman at the mill
t: From the palace to the mill
p: Exodus 11:5 and 12:29 join the two ends of Egypt's society.
b: Exodus 11:5 has "from the firstborn of Pharaoh on his throne to the firstborn of the slave woman at the hand mill," and Exodus 12:29 has "the firstborn of the captive in the pit-house." Jubilees combines them: a woman who is both captive and at the mill. No house, high or low, escapes (49:5).

a: to pass over it
p: The Ge'ez verb means "pass by." It carries the Hebrew wordplay of pesach, "pass over."
b: The Ge'ez yətʿadäwu means "pass by" or "cross over," and the same verb returns in 49:4 and 49:14 ("moved"). It carries the sense of the Hebrew pasach in Exodus 12:13: "I will see the blood and pass over you." In Jubilees the ones who pass over are the destroying powers, not God himself.

a: down to the dog
p: Exodus 11:7 says not a dog would growl at Israel.
b: Exodus 11:7: "But against all the Israelites not a dog will sharpen its tongue, against man or animal." Jubilees turns the saying around: the plague did not destroy any life in Israel, "from animal to human, down to the dog."

a: drinking wine
p: Exodus does not mention wine. Charles called this the oldest mention of wine at the Passover meal.
b: Exodus 12:8 names meat, unleavened bread and bitter herbs. Charles 1902 wrote that this verse "seems to be the earliest reference to the use of wine at the Passover feast," pointing to the Mishnah's later rule of cups (Mishnah Pesahim 10). In the Gospels Jesus takes a cup at his last Passover meal (Luke 22:17-20; Mark 14:23-25). Jubilees also has Israel praising and thanking God at the meal, a step toward the later Passover service.

a: Do not move it from one day to another
p: Jubilees insists the Passover stay on its day, a point tied to its 364-day calendar.
b: Jubilees repeats this command three times (49:7, 49:14, and the "set time" of 49:10). Charles 1902 compares the same wording for the Feast of Weeks (6:20-22) and admits the exact sense is hard (the Latin is corrupt here). One reason fits the book's calendar: in a year of exactly 364 days, 52 weeks with nothing left over, every date falls on the same day of the week every year (compare 1 Enoch 72:32, "The year comes to exactly 364 days"). A moon-based calendar, which needs added months, would move the feasts. On the calendar debate, see 6:23-38 and the calendar topic.

a: engraved on the heavenly tablets
p: The Passover law is one of the laws Jubilees says were written on the heavenly tablets before Sinai.
b: Jubilees often says a law is "engraved" or "written" on ṣəlatä sämay, "the heavenly tablets" (see 3:10). The point is that the Passover is not a custom Israel made up but a law of heaven, given to Israel "forever." Exodus 12:14 also calls it "a rule for all time."

a: clean and close by
t: The man who skips the Passover
p: Taken from Numbers 9:13.
b: Numbers 9:13: "But a man who is clean and not on a journey, and still does not keep the Passover, is to be cut off from his people. He failed to present the LORD's offering at its time, so he will carry the penalty of his sin." Jubilees follows it closely, with "close by" (Ge'ez qrub) for "not on a journey." Charles 1902 compares the rabbis' rule that set a distance from Jerusalem within which a clean man had to come.

a: between the evenings
p: The Hebrew phrase of Exodus 12:6 was argued over. Jubilees defines it: from the last third of the day into the night.
b: Exodus 12:6 says to slaughter the lamb "between the two evenings" (Hebrew bein ha-ʿarbayim). Jubilees explains: the day has three parts, two of light and one of evening, so the time runs "from the third part of the day to the third part of the night," and 49:12 narrows the killing to "the edge of evening." Charles 1902 sets this beside later debates: the rabbinic practice of slaughtering in the afternoon (Josephus gives the ninth to the eleventh hour, Jewish War 6.9.3), and the Samaritan and Karaite practice of slaughtering between sunset and dark. Deuteronomy 16:6 says "in the evening, as the sun goes down."

a: until the third part of the night
t: Compared with the Bible: the meal's end
p: Exodus 12:10 allows eating until morning. Jubilees ends the meal at the third part of the night.
b: Exodus 12:10 says, "Do not leave any of it until morning. Whatever is left of it until morning, burn in the fire." Jubilees sets an earlier limit: the meal ends with the first third of the night, about ten o'clock by Charles's reckoning, and the leftovers are burned from then on. Charles 1902 notes that the Mishnah set midnight as the limit (Berakhot 1:1). The rule is stricter than the Bible's but not against it.

a: no bone of it may be broken
t: No bone broken: Exodus to the cross
p: Exodus 12:46 forbids breaking the lamb's bones. John 19:36 sees the rule fulfilled in Jesus.
b: The rule is from Exodus 12:46 ("do not break any of its bones") and Numbers 9:12. Jubilees adds a reason the Bible does not give: "For no bone of the Israelites will be crushed." The lamb's unbroken body stands for Israel kept whole. The Gospel of John reads the same rule of Jesus' body on the cross: "For all this took place to make the Scripture come true: 'No bone of his will be broken'" (John 19:36; compare Psalm 34:20). Paul calls Christ "our Passover" (1 Corinthians 5:7). Jubilees is not a source for John, but it shows how much weight Jews of the time gave to this small rule.

a: with care
p: Ge'ez bäʾästäḥämmo, "with care." Charles traced it to the Greek for Exodus 12:11's "in haste."
b: The Ge'ez bäʾästäḥämmo comes from the verb that Leslau's dictionary gives as "take pains, do something with care, be assiduous." Charles 1902 rendered it "with diligence" and explained it as the Greek σπουδαίως, which the Greek Bible uses for the Hebrew be-chippazon, "in haste" (Exodus 12:11, "Eat it in a rush"). So behind the Ge'ez "with care" may lie the haste of the first Passover. In 49:23, Charles notes, the Hebrew phrase is rendered more literally.

a: no plague will come on them
p: Keeping the Passover rightly brings safety for the whole year.
b: Exodus 12:13 promised that "no blow will fall on you" on the night of the Exodus. Jubilees extends the promise: each year the Passover is kept "at its time in every way," no plague will strike Israel that year. Charles 1902 notes that the same idea, no harm on the day of a right Passover, stands behind the words about bones in 49:13 as the Latin has them. Kept wrongly, at the wrong time, the feast loses this promise: one more reason the book cares so much about the date.

a: outside the sanctuary of the Lord
t: Compared with the Bible: from the house to the sanctuary
p: Exodus 12 has the Passover in every home. Jubilees, like Deuteronomy 16, allows it only at the sanctuary.
b: In Egypt every family ate the lamb in its own house (Exodus 12:3-4; Exodus 12:46, "It must be eaten inside one house"). Deuteronomy 16:5-7 moves the sacrifice to "the place the LORD your God will choose." Jubilees takes Deuteronomy's side and goes further: the meat must be eaten "in front of the sanctuary" (49:16), in its courtyard (49:20), by men twenty and older (49:17). Charles 1902 notes that the Mishnah later allowed the meat to be eaten anywhere in Jerusalem, because of the crowds. Since AD 70, with no temple, Jews keep the Passover with a meal (the seder) but no lamb sacrifice, in keeping with the Bible's rule of one place.

a: from twenty years old and up
p: Charles notes the rabbis set the age at fourteen. Twenty is the census age of Exodus 30:14.
b: Charles 1902 wrote that rabbinic tradition set the age at fourteen, and that Jubilees' twenty probably comes from the census rule of Exodus 30:14 ("from twenty years old and up") and Numbers 1:3. Luke 2:42 shows a family taking a boy along at twelve: "When he turned twelve, they made the trip up, as the festival's custom was." Jubilees speaks only of who must eat it in the sanctuary, not of who may come.

a: in one of their tribes
p: Before the temple, the tabernacle stood in one tribe's land, at Shiloh (Joshua 18:1).
b: The Ge'ez śärawitomu is a plural of särwe, "army" (Leslau), so literally "their hosts": Israel's tribes counted as armies (compare Numbers 2). Charles 1902 translated "tribes," and the Plain English Translation follows him. The book looks ahead to the time when the tabernacle stood in the land before the temple was built. Joshua 18:1 says, "The whole community of the Israelites came together at Shiloh, and there they set up the tent of meeting." The Passover at Gilgal (Joshua 5:10) came even before that.

a: as the sun goes down
t: At sunset, in the chosen place
p: Deuteronomy 16:6 gives the same hour and the same place.
b: "Sacrifice the Passover only at the place the LORD your God will choose to make his name live there. Do it in the evening, as the sun goes down, at the time of day you came out of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 16:6). Jubilees speaks of a "house" built "in the Lord's name," which points to Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:29; 2 Chronicles 35:1-19) without naming Jerusalem.

a: bring its blood up onto the base of the altar
t: Compared with the Bible: the Passover as a temple sacrifice
p: Exodus puts the blood on the doorposts. Jubilees, like Chronicles, puts it on the altar.
b: In Egypt the blood went on "the two doorposts and on the beam above the door" (Exodus 12:7). Once there is a sanctuary, Jubilees treats the Passover like other sacrifices: blood at the altar's base, fat burned on the altar (compare Leviticus 3:3-5 and Leviticus 4:7). This is how Chronicles describes Josiah's Passover: "They slaughtered the Passover, and the priests splashed the blood they took from their hands" (2 Chronicles 35:11; compare 2 Chronicles 30:16).

a: They may not keep the Passover
p: Ge'ez "they are not able." Charles traced it, through the Greek, to the Hebrew of Deuteronomy 16:5, "you may not."
b: The Ge'ez ʾiykəlu literally means "they are not able." Charles 1902 explained that the Greek translator (and the Latin after him) rendered a Hebrew "you may not" as "you cannot," the same over-literal rendering the Greek Bible has in Deuteronomy 16:5: "You may not sacrifice the Passover in just any of the towns the LORD your God is giving you." The sense is a prohibition, so the Plain English Translation says "may not."

a: the Feast of Unleavened Bread
p: The second half of the festival: Exodus 12:15-20; 34:18; Leviticus 23:6-8.
b: "Keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. For seven days eat flat bread made with no yeast" (Exodus 34:18). The daily offering for the seven days comes from Numbers 28:17-25. Jubilees calls them "seven days of joy" (compare Deuteronomy 16:3, which calls the bread "the bread of hardship"). The Ge'ez bäʿalä naʾt is literally "the feast of unleavened bread."

a: Tell them its year, every year, and its day among the days
p: The Ge'ez is literally "its year for each year and its day for the days." The manuscripts and the Latin differ.
b: The Ge'ez reads ʿamäto lälä ʿamät wäʿläto läʿlätat, "its year for each year, and its day for the days." Charles 1902 found the words "and the day of its days" corrupt and preferred the Latin "in tempore dierum suorum," "at the time of its days," and notes that two of his manuscripts read "every year" alone. The sense either way is that Moses must fix the date for Israel each year.
orig: ዓመቶ ፡ ለለ ፡ ዓመት ፡ ወዕለቶ ፡ ለዕለታት (ʿamäto lälä ʿamät wäʿläto läʿlätat)

a: until you crossed the sea into the Wilderness of Shur
t: The feast that ended at the sea
p: Jubilees makes the seven days of unleavened bread the days of the march to the sea.
b: Exodus 15:22 says that after the sea, Israel "went out into the wilderness of Shur." By Jubilees' timetable (48:15-16) Israel left on the fifteenth, Mastema was loosed on the nineteenth, and the sea was crossed by the end of the feast, "for you finished it on the shore of the sea." Exodus 13:6-8 ties the seven days of unleavened bread to the Exodus, but does not date the crossing.

a: the Wilderness of Sinai, which is between Elim and Sinai
p: Exodus 16:1 says the Wilderness of Sin lies between Elim and Sinai. The Ge'ez says Sinai; Charles calls it a slip.
b: Exodus 16:1: "Leaving Elim, the whole community of Israelites arrived in the Wilderness of Sin, between Elim and Sinai." That is where the Sabbath was first given, with the manna (Exodus 16:23-30). The Ge'ez says gädamä sina, "the wilderness of Sina(i)," which makes the place lie between Elim and itself. Charles 1902 judged "Sinai" a corruption of "Sin," an easy slip since the names look alike.

a: the Sabbaths of the land
p: Leviticus 25 gives the land a Sabbath year every seventh year, and a Jubilee after seven of them.
b: Leviticus 25:2: "When you come into the land that I am giving you, the land is to rest, a Sabbath for the LORD." Leviticus 25:8 counts "seven Sabbaths of years" to the Jubilee. Jubilees says these laws were told on Sinai (Leviticus 25:1, "The LORD spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai") but that the year to begin counting was held back until Israel entered the land.

a: The land too will keep its Sabbaths
p: Leviticus 26:34 says the land will make up its Sabbaths when Israel is in exile.
b: Leviticus 26:34: "Then the land will make up for its Sabbaths, all the days it lies desolate while you are in your enemies' land." 2 Chronicles 36:21 reads the exile that way. Jubilees speaks only of the good side: while Israel lives on the land, the land keeps its rest.

a: forty-nine jubilees from the days of Adam to this day
p: 49 jubilees, one week and two years bring Sinai to year 2410. Forty more years make 2450: fifty jubilees.
b: Forty-nine jubilees (49 x 49 = 2,401 years), one week (7) and two years make the year 2410 from creation, the year Moses hears these words on Sinai. Forty more years in the wilderness bring Israel to the Jordan in 2450, which is exactly fifty jubilees of forty-nine years. Charles prints both figures. He also notes that Jubilees counts a jubilee as forty-nine years, as one rabbi did, while most Jewish writers counted fifty (Leviticus 25:10, "Make the fiftieth year holy").

a: until they cross over into the land of Canaan
t: Claude's reading: the whole of history as one Jubilee
p: If Israel enters the land in the fiftieth jubilee, the entry itself is a Jubilee: going home to the family land.
b: This is Claude's reading of the numbers. In Leviticus 25:10 the Jubilee is the year when "Each of you will go back to his own holding." By Jubilees' count, Israel crosses the Jordan exactly at the end of fifty jubilees from creation (50:4), into land that the book says was given by lot to Shem's line (8:12-21) and taken by Canaan wrongly (10:29-34). The conquest then is not a seizure but a return home in the great Jubilee of history. The book does not say this in so many words; it lets the numbers say it.

a: until Israel is made clean
t: A cleansed Israel in a clean land
p: The book ends with a hope like that of 1:23-29 and 23:26-31: no satan (no accuser or enemy at all; see 46:2), no evil, a land made clean.
b: The jubilees will keep turning until Israel is clean of sin and lives safely, with "no satan" (compare 46:2 and 23:29). Charles 1902 read this as the book's hope of a messianic kingdom that comes about gradually, as in 1:29 and 23:26-28. Christian readers hear echoes of Revelation 21-22 and of Satan's binding (Revelation 20:2-3); Jewish readers, of the prophets' promises of a cleansed land (Ezekiel 36:25-28; Zechariah 13:2, where God will remove "the spirit of uncleanness from the land").

a: the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God
p: From Exodus 20:9-10. The book that began with the Sabbath at creation (2:17-33) ends with it.
b: Exodus 20:10: "but the seventh day is a Sabbath for the LORD your God. Do no work on it." Jubilees ends where its account of creation peaked: the Sabbath kept by God and the angels from the first week (2:17-33). The last chapter turns that story into law with penalties.

a: Anyone who does any work on it is to die
p: The penalty comes from Exodus 31:14-15 and 35:2. Jubilees applies it to a long list of acts.
b: Exodus 35:2: "Anyone who does work on it must be put to death." Exodus 31:14 adds, "Anyone who treats it as common must be put to death." Numbers 15:32-36 tells of a man stoned for gathering wood. Charles 1902 notes that Jubilees takes this penalty for "any and every breach" of the Sabbath. The list that follows goes beyond the Bible: some items have a basis in Scripture (travel, Exodus 16:29; trading, Nehemiah 13:15-17; carrying a load, Jeremiah 17:21-22, "Do not haul a load on the sabbath day"), and some do not (relations with one's wife, drawing water).

a: who lies with his wife
p: Jubilees forbids marital relations on the Sabbath. The rabbis later encouraged them; the Beta Israel kept the strict rule.
b: The Ge'ez zäysäkb məslä bəʾsit is "who lies with a woman" (bəʾsit also means "wife"); the setting shows a man's own wife is meant. Charles 1902 notes that the Mishnah and Talmud took the opposite view and encouraged relations on the Sabbath eve, while the strict rule was kept by the Samaritans, the Karaite Jews and "the Abyssinian Falashas," the Beta Israel of Ethiopia, who held Jubilees in honor. The Bible itself has no such law. The closest passages are the temporary rules at Sinai (Exodus 19:15) and the uncleanness of Leviticus 15:18.

a: setting out on a journey on it
p: From Exodus 16:29. The rabbis set a "Sabbath limit" of 2,000 cubits; Acts 1:12 knows it.
b: The rule grows from Exodus 16:29: "On the seventh day, each of you stay put in your own spot. No one is to go out from where he is." Charles 1902 notes that later Jewish law allowed a walk of two thousand cubits, the "Sabbath limit" (Mishnah Eruvin 4-5), and that Josephus quotes a rule against traveling on the Sabbath. Acts 1:12 measures the Mount of Olives from Jerusalem as "as far as a person may walk on the Sabbath."

a: whoever draws water on it that he did not get ready for himself on the sixth day
p: The manna rule of Exodus 16:23 is extended to water and other needs.
b: Before the first Sabbath, Moses told the people, "Bake whatever you plan to bake, and boil whatever you plan to boil" (Exodus 16:23), and God gave "two days' bread" on the sixth day (Exodus 16:29). Jubilees applies the same principle to drawing water and, in 50:9, to all work: what the Sabbath needs must be ready the day before. Charles 1902 found the clause awkward here and notes that the Karaite Jews also forbade drawing water.

a: a day of the holy kingdom
p: Ge'ez ʿəlätä mängəśt qədsət. The Sabbath is a foretaste of God's reign, a royal day for Israel.
b: The phrase ʿəlätä mängəśt qədsət is unusual. It may echo Exodus 19:6, where Israel is to be "a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" (the book quotes it in 16:18 and 33:20), so that the Sabbath is the day when Israel lives as God's royal and holy people. Isaiah 58:13 calls the Sabbath "a delight" and "the LORD's holy day honored."

a: burning incense and bringing offerings and sacrifices
p: The Sabbath offerings of Numbers 28:9-10 are the one work allowed. Jesus points to the same fact.
b: Numbers 28:9-10 orders a Sabbath burnt offering "on top of the regular burnt offering." So the priests worked every Sabbath. Jubilees allows this work only, in the sanctuary (50:11). Jesus uses the same fact to answer the Pharisees: "Or have you not read in the Law that every Sabbath the priests in the temple treat the Sabbath as common, and yet they are blameless?" (Matthew 12:5). Charles 1902 makes the same comparison.

a: to make atonement for Israel
p: The daily and Sabbath offerings "make atonement" for Israel and keep a "reminder" before God.
b: The Ge'ez yastäsrəyu is "make atonement, obtain forgiveness." Jubilees treats the regular sacrifices as covering Israel's sin day after day, a "pleasing reminder" before God. Numbers 28:22 speaks of an offering "to make atonement for you," and Exodus 29:38-42 sets the lamb of every morning and evening.

a: lights a fire
p: Exodus 35:3 forbids kindling a fire. The man who gathered sticks was stoned (Numbers 15:32-36).
b: "On the Sabbath day you must not kindle a fire in any of your homes" (Exodus 35:3). Charles 1902 links this to the man who gathered wood in Numbers 15:32-36 and to the Mishnah's list of forbidden works (Shabbat 7:2), which also forbids plowing, harvesting and killing an animal. Exodus 34:21 already forbids plowing and harvesting: "Even at plowing time and at harvest you are to stop."

a: rides on any animal
p: Not in the Bible. Charles cites later Jewish law, and a Talmud story of a man stoned for riding a horse in Greek times.
b: The Bible says nothing about riding or sailing on the Sabbath. Charles 1902 notes that the Mishnah forbids riding an animal on a feast day (Betzah 5:2), and that the Talmud (Sanhedrin 46a) tells of a man stoned in the days of Greek rule for riding a horse on the Sabbath. He took that harsh time as the background of several of these laws.

a: fasts
p: The Sabbath is for eating and drinking (50:9-10). Judith keeps the rule.
b: Since the Sabbath is a feast for eating and drinking (50:9-10), fasting breaks it. Charles 1902 points to Judith, who "fasted every day of her widowhood, except the days before the Sabbaths and the Sabbaths" (Judith 8:6). The Bible itself has no law against fasting on the Sabbath, though Nehemiah 8:9-12 forbids mourning on a holy day.

a: makes war on the Sabbath day
t: War on the Sabbath and the Maccabees
p: Jubilees forbids all fighting on the Sabbath. Early in the Maccabean revolt, a thousand Jews died rather than fight.
b: The Bible has no law against fighting on the Sabbath. But at the start of the Maccabean revolt, loyal Jews hiding in the wilderness would not fight on the Sabbath, and "They died, with their wives and children and animals, about a thousand human lives" (1 Maccabees 2:38). Mattathias then decided: "Whoever comes to make war on us on the Sabbath day, we will fight him face to face" (1 Maccabees 2:41). Charles 1902 notes that the ban on all warfare was observed literally before and during the outbreak of the Maccabean wars, until Mattathias allowed defense, and traces how the narrower rule (defense only) later cost the Jews when Pompey besieged Jerusalem. Scholars who date the book use this verse; the dating views are on the book's opening pages.

a: the tablets that he gave into my hands
p: The angel writes from tablets God gave him. Moses' stone tablets are another thing.
b: The book closes its frame. In 1:27-29 God told the angel of the presence to dictate to Moses from the tablets of the divisions of the years, and in 2:1 the angel began. Now he says he has written "the laws of each time" from "the tablets that he gave into my hands." These are the heavenly tablets (49:8), not Moses' stone tablets (Exodus 24:12; Exodus 31:18).

a: Here ends the account of the division of the days
p: The closing line names the book: Kufale, "the division (of the days)," its Ge'ez title.
b: The Ge'ez colophon reads täfäṣämä bäzyä nägär zäkufale mäwaʿl, "here is completed the word of the division of the days." Kufale, "division," is the book's Ge'ez name, and the prologue (1:0) opens with "the divisions of the times." The Damascus Document seems to refer to a book of the "divisions of the times" by jubilees and weeks (CD 16:2-4), which many take to be this book (see the book's introduction).
